title: Context engineering
summary: Context engineering is choosing what enters the model's window at every step: instructions, tool definitions, memory, retrieved data, history and tool results. The aim is the smallest set of high-signal tokens that makes the next step succeed.
useIf: An agent runs many steps, uses many tools or large tool results, or the bill and latency are dominated by input tokens.
avoidIf: Never skip it for long agent loops. For one short chat turn with a small prompt there is little to engineer.

explain.md: Anthropic frames context as a finite resource with diminishing returns: the model has an **attention budget**, and every token competes with the others. The goal is the smallest set of high-signal tokens that makes the next step succeed [[r6]]. Cognition calls context engineering effectively the number one job of an agent builder [[r3]]. Five levers matter: what is in the prompt, in which order, how large tool results are, what history you keep and what you load only on demand.

explain.title: The window budget
explain.expr: used = system + tools + memory + history + retrieval + tool_results + reserved_output     (stay under the window)

vars.v: tool definitions, resent on every request
room kept for the answer and any reasoning tokens

explain.example: System 2,000 + 60 tools x 350 + memory 1,500 + 30 turns x 800 + 5 chunks x 900 + tool results 28,000 + output 6,000 = **87,000** tokens in a 100,000 window, leaving 13,000.

explain.title: A cache-friendly prompt layout
explain.alt: From top to bottom the prompt holds stable system instructions, tool definitions and memory, then append-only history, then volatile retrieval and tool results, then reserved output. The stable prefix can be cached.
explain.src:
flowchart TB
  A[System instructions: stable] --> B[Tool definitions: stable, fixed order]
  B --> C[Memory: stable per session]
  C --> D[History: append-only]
  D --> E[Volatile retrieval and tool results]
  E --> F[Reserved output]

explain.md: Order is a cost lever. Manus calls the KV-cache hit rate the single most important production metric, reports an average input to output ratio near 100 to 1, and quotes cached input at $0.30 per million tokens against $3 uncached for one Claude model in 2025 (check current pricing). Its rules: keep the prefix stable, so a timestamp at the start of the system prompt kills hits, make context append-only, serialise deterministically, and mask tools instead of removing them mid-run [[r7]]. Placement is also a quality lever: accuracy is highest when relevant text sits at the start or end of the input and lowest in the middle [[r39]], so keep critical constraints near the edges and recite the current plan near the end, as Manus does with a todo file [[r7]].

Load data on demand. Keep lightweight identifiers such as paths, queries and links, and fetch content with tools when needed [[r6]]. Trim tool results to the fields the model needs and keep a pointer to the rest.

explain.intro: Illustrative planner, not a tokenizer: sizes, windows and the cache discount are your inputs, not vendor figures. Load the Tool-heavy agent preset and apply tool search, then compare summarising with dropping on the research preset, and switch the prompt to the cache-friendly order.

whereToUse: Any agent that loops over tools for more than a handful of steps
Assistants with large tool catalogs from several teams
RAG assistants where retrieved chunks compete with history for space
Cost reviews where input tokens dominate the invoice
Latency work: shorter, cache-friendly prompts shorten time to first token

use: The agent takes many steps and history grows
Tool definitions or tool results are large
Input tokens, not output, drive cost and latency
avoid: Over-compressing early, which drops details that later steps need
Rewriting history every turn, which breaks cache reuse
Chasing a larger window instead of trimming what you send
flips: Tool results are the bulk: trim or clear them first
Tool definitions are the bulk: load tools on demand with tool search
History is the bulk and stays relevant: summarise with pinned facts and offload detail to files

pitfalls.symptom: Cached-input share collapsed after a prompt change
pitfalls.cause: A volatile value such as a timestamp or retrieval block sits before stable content
pitfalls.fix: Move volatile segments to the end, serialise tools and JSON deterministically and keep history append-only.

pitfalls.symptom: The request overflows or quality drops before the user speaks
pitfalls.cause: Dozens of tool definitions are loaded on every call
pitfalls.fix: Load a small set of tools plus a search tool, and de-duplicate overlapping tools.

pitfalls.symptom: The agent forgets an early instruction in a long run
pitfalls.cause: It sits in the middle of a long context where recall is weakest [[r39]]
pitfalls.fix: Pin instructions near the start, recite the current goal near the end and compact history.

scenarios.title: Cache hits fell after a release
scenarios.situation: After a prompt change, input cost per request rose sharply and time to first token worsened. Nothing else changed. The release added the current date and a retrieved snippet near the top of the system prompt.
constraints: Cost and latency regression is measured
unknowns: What does the cached-token field show per request?
Is tool order stable between requests?
scenarios.question: What do you change?

options.name: Move the date and retrieval to the end, keep the prefix stable and serialise tools in a fixed order
options.why: Caches reuse the longest identical prefix, so a volatile value early in the prompt defeats them.
options.tradeoff: Instructions that depend on the date must read it from later in the prompt.

options.name: Switch to a larger model
options.why: It does not touch the cause and raises per-token cost.
options.tradeoff: Right only if quality, not cost, were the problem.

options.name: Disable caching to avoid inconsistency
options.tradeoff: You pay full price for every token and give up latency savings.

flips.if: Prompts are shorter than the provider's minimum cacheable length
flips.then: Caching will not apply, so focus on trimming instead.

flips.if: Retrieval must precede instructions for quality
flips.then: Test the quality gain against the lost cache share.

scenarios.title: A tool-heavy agent overflows
scenarios.situation: An agent exposes eighty tools from several teams and long tool outputs. Requests approach the window limit, and tool choice has become unreliable.
constraints: No budget to move to a bigger window
unknowns: How much of the window do tool definitions take?
Can large outputs be reduced to key fields?
scenarios.question: What do you do first?

options.name: Load a few tools plus a tool search, trim tool results to key fields and clear stale results with pointers
options.why: It attacks the two largest segments with the least risk, and tool search also reduces overlap errors.
options.tradeoff: An extra search round trip and the chance of missing a similar tool.

options.name: Summarise the whole history every five steps
options.why: Frees space as the run grows.
options.tradeoff: Loses exact details, costs an extra call and rewrites history, which breaks cache reuse.

options.name: Raise the window by moving to a larger-context model
options.why: Quality degrades with length and cost rises, while the overlap problem remains.
options.tradeoff: Reasonable for one-off tasks that truly need the whole input.

flips.then: Offload to files and summarise, after clearing results.

flips.if: Tool sets differ by trust boundary

scenarios.takeaway: Trim the biggest, safest segment first.

quiz.q: Which prompt order is most friendly to prefix caching?
options: Retrieved chunks, system prompt, tools, history
Current date, system prompt, tools, history
System prompt, tools, memory, history, retrieval and tool results
quiz.explain: Stable segments go first, history is append-only and volatile segments go last, so the longest identical prefix is reused. The other orders put changing content ahead of stable content. [[r7]]

quiz.q: System 2,000 + 60 tools at 350 tokens + memory 1,500 + 30 turns at 800 + 5 chunks at 900 + tool results 28,000 + reserved output 6,000. How many tokens of headroom remain in a 100,000 token window?
quiz.hint: Sum all segments, then subtract from the window.
quiz.explain: 2,000 + 21,000 + 1,500 + 24,000 + 4,500 + 28,000 + 6,000 = 87,000, so headroom is 13,000. Remember the soft quality limit sits below the hard window.

quiz.q: Which practices in an agent's prompt assembly are bugs for cache hit rate?
options: A timestamp at the start of the system prompt
Appending new turns to the end of history
Serialising tools in a different order on each request
Keeping the system prompt unchanged across turns
quiz.explain: A leading timestamp and unstable tool or JSON ordering change the prefix and defeat caching. Append-only history and an unchanged system prompt preserve the prefix. [[r7]]

flashcards.front: What is the attention budget idea?
flashcards.back: Context is finite with diminishing returns. Aim for the smallest set of high-signal tokens for the next step [[r6]].
Stable prefix (no leading timestamp), append-only context, deterministic serialisation, and mask tools instead of removing them [[r7]].

flashcards.front: Where does the model recall best in long input?
flashcards.back: At the start and end of the input, with the lowest recall in the middle (Lost in the Middle) [[r39]].
